analysis.one_liner: Caps federal farm subsidy checks at $125,000 per person and tightens rules so only real farmers collect.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: introduced with no cosponsors, it died in a House Agriculture subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal farm programs send billions in payments each year, and the rules let some large operations collect multiple checks. This bill would cap payments at $125,000 per person per year ($250,000 for a married couple), limit how much could come from trade-distorting marketing loan gains, and tighten the definition of who counts as an actively engaged farmer so absentee managers and passive investors could not multiply their subsidy checks. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who fund farm subsidies would bear less of the cost, since the cap and the tightened 'actively engaged' rules would cut checks to the largest recipients and to people who qualify only on paper [S2][S3]. Small and mid-size family farms that receive payments well below the cap would be largely untouched.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a $125,000 annual cap per person or legal entity on commodity program payments — no more than $50,000 in other commodity payments plus $75,000 in marketing loan gains and loan deficiency payments [S2][S3].
Doubles the limit to $250,000 for married couples, while requiring couples who were each farming separately before marriage to be treated as separate persons for their own operations [S3].

Tightens the 'actively engaged in farming' test by removing 'active personal management' as a standalone qualification, and creates a narrow farm-manager class that only one person per operation can use, with rules barring management contributions used to qualify in more than one operation — closing a known route for people to collect multiple checks [S2][S3].
Directs the Secretary of Agriculture to write rules ensuring irrevocable trusts receiving payments are legitimate entities and not created to dodge the payment cap [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The largest farm operations and entities that currently stack multiple subsidy payments, including operations that qualify extra recipients as 'managers' rather than working farmers, would see their federal checks reduced [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Commodity payments cushion farms against sharp price drops, and an honest supporter must acknowledge that capping large operations' payments means less federal backstop for the biggest farms in bad years [S3].

The married-couple limit is twice the individual limit, which creates different outcomes for unmarried partners running a farm together and could push operations into restructuring purely to fit the rules [S3].

The revised farm-manager rules add new determinations for the Agriculture Department to police, and critics of payment limits generally argue such tests are hard to enforce and generate paperwork without changing who actually farms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade is straightforward: less federal support for the largest, often best-capitalized operations in exchange for lower taxpayer cost and tighter rules against collecting checks on paper rather than in the field. Its main weakness is design, not principle — the manager rules and trust rules depend on discretionary determinations by the Agriculture Department, and the cap could push sophisticated operations into restructuring rather than reducing payments. But the bill never advanced far enough for those questions to be tested in a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee, and died there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeff Fortenberry introduced the Farm Program Integrity Act of 2013 on May 9, 2013 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Agriculture Committee, and on May 22, 2013 to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management [S5].
The bill received no further action and expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest farm subsidy recipients and absentee investors collecting multiple checks are better off, since nothing limited their payments.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large subsidy recipients keep unlimited-style payments

for.name: Rep. Jeff Fortenberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tighten farm payment limits and the actively-engaged rules; no colleagues joined him.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.role: Committee of referral — chaired by Rep. Frank Lucas (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; it sat in the General Farm Commodities and Risk Management subcommittee until Congress ended.

against.name: House farm subsidy recipients and agribusiness interests
against.what_they_did: Payment-limit tightening routinely draws opposition from large farm operations and commodity groups; no such opposition appears in the record because the bill never reached a hearing.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill's sole sponsor was a Republican with no cosponsors, so no party split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Large commodity farm operations and farm entities
industries.note: The bill would cap their federal payments at $125,000 per person and block multiple 'manager' designations used to stack checks [S2][S3]. Their revenue from federal programs would shrink, and taxpayers would save the difference.

industries.industry: Passive landowners and absentee investors in farming operations
industries.note: Tightened actively-engaged rules would disqualify people who qualify only through management or paper contributions rather than labor [S3].
